newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to send Congress "America Reads" plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to send Congress "America Reads" plan.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Saturday he would soon send legislation to Congress that would begin funding his five-year, $2.75 billion programme to help mobilise an army of volunteers to teach children to read.

Clinton made the announcement in a weekly radio address devoted to encouraging citizens to make volunteer service a part of their lives, a day before he attends a national service summit in Philadelphia.
With him at the summit will be former presidents George Bush, Jimmy Carter and Gerald Ford and retired Gen. Colin Powell, along with thousands of volunteer advocates from across the country.

"Citizen service is neighbour helping neighbour," Clinton said. "It's part-time volunteers and full-time community service workers. It's communities coming together to solve common problems. And it is an essential part of what it means to be an American."

Clinton said he would send to Congress on Monday the America Reads Challenge Act, which would fund 25,000 reading specialists and tutor coordinators, including 11,000 members of his national service programme, AmeriCorps.
The aim is to mobilise one million volunteer reading tutors to provide reading help before and after school to three million children at 20,000 schools.
Clinton, in a goal he outlined during his 1996 re-election campaign, said he wanted to make sure that every 8-year-old in America can pick up a book and say, "I read this all by myself."

The president's plan will ask the Republican-controlled Congress to approve $460 million for the 1998 fiscal year starting Oct. 1, White House spokesman Barry Toiv said. This would be the first stage of a five-year, $2.75 billion programme.

In the heat of last year's election battle, the campaign of then-Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole attacked the plan, saying Clinton should embark on a fundamental reform of education and confront teachers' unions instead of announcing "a new government programme and a new pot of money for the unions."
Toiv said Clinton's national literacy campaign would be paid for as part of his overall plan for balancing the federal budget by 2002.
"Obviously to make investments of this kind, especially when you're achieving a balanced budget, it requires that you be very prudent about spending elsewhere," he said.

As evidence that the programme is needed, a White House fact sheet cited studies showing students who cannot read well and independently by the end of the third grade are less likely to succeed in school and more likely to drop out.

It said 40 percent of fourth graders scored below the basic level on the 1994 National Assessment of Educational Progress. The White House said studies have shown well-designed tutoring programmes result in student gains in reading.
Clinton urged Americans interesting in becoming volunteer tutors to call the Education Department's hotline, 1-800-USA-LEARN, or contact the local elementary school or library.

The Philadelphia event, dubbed "The Presidents' Summit for America's Future," aims to develop ways for volunteers to help create better living conditions for 2 million of an estimated 15 million "at risk" children by 2000. Clinton is to attend events there Sunday and Monday.
